newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu heads home to new talks, new pressures.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu heads home to new talks, new pressures.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returns on Monday from a U.S. visit to face a tightening political vice at home over the thorniest issues dividing Jews and Palestinians.
Israeli and Palestinian teams were to meet in a new round of talks on implementing interim agreements signed since their landmark peace deal in 1993.

Overshadowing the meeting was the planned resumption in March of "final status" talks on such core issues as the shape of Israeli-Palestinian borders and the fate of Arab East Jerusalem, Jewish settlements and Palestinian refugees in exile.

As the interim round was formally launched on Sunday in Kibbutz Maale Hahamisha, a collective village west of Jerusalem, Palestinians warned Netanyahu to resist the appeals of Israeli rightists to speed Jewish settlement construction.
"The Israeli government should not pre-empt these (final status) negotiations by trying to put fait accompli policies on the ground," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters.
"All these activities, whether confiscation of land, settlements, Judaisation of Jerusalem, must cease, must stop immediately."
Israel's chief negotiator, Foreign Minister David Levy, fired off a warning of his own, saying final status issues would not be tolerated at the interim talks.
"No question may be raised that from our standpoint is known to be a landmine in the way of progress," Levy told reporters.
Prodded by Washington, Netanyahu gave some momentum to a foundering peace process last month by approving a long-delayed army pullout from 80 percent of the West Bank town of Hebron.
But the Hebron deal sounded alarm bells among the Israeli rightists who helped the prime minister to an upset election victory in May.

"We feel humiliated," said settler spokesman Noam Arnon, after disgruntled Jews in Hebron complained to Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai that the government had not met promises to bolster settlement in the town.

Israeli hardliners were further distressed by a report that Netanyahu would withhold approval "for the near future" of the building of Har Homa, a Jewish neighbourhood in politically explosive East Jerusalem.
An aide to Netanyahu denied the report, by Israel's Channel Two Television.

Washington has long viewed settlements as an obstacle to peace and Palestinians denounce them as a provocation. But Netanyahu's Likud party and its rightist coalition partners have long championed settlement activity.
The final status talks, to resume in mid-March after a formal launch last May, are to be concluded by May 1999.

The agenda for the interim talks includes arrangements for Palestinian sea and air ports, a "safe passage" between the West Bank and Gaza, economic, civil and financial affairs and "people to people" grass-roots cooperation projects, officials said.
